title: Low-nonlinearity advantage of hollow-core fiber for wavelength multiplexing of quantum entanglement and classical DWDM signals
authors: Hikaru Shimizu, Arisa Ohno, Mao Miyasugi, Yumeno Seki, Naoyuki Funaoka, Yukari Takada, Aruto Hosaka, Shun Fujii, Hiroyuki Tsuda, Masahiro Takeoka
abstract: Coexistence of classical and quantum light in optical fiber is a key requirement for scalable quantum networks. However, it is fundamentally limited by nonlinear crosstalk from intense classical signals. Hollow-core fiber (HCF), with its intrinsically low optical nonlinearity, offers a promising solution. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the coexistence of polarization-entangled photons with dense wavelength-division multiplexed (DWDM) classical signals with a total launch power of 11.2 dBm, and perform a direct comparison between equal-length single-mode fiber (SMF) and photonic-bandgap-based HCF deployed in a campus network. We observe that HCF suppresses background noise by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to SMF, while preserving high-fidelity entanglement distribution. Our results provide clear experimental evidence of the advantage of HCF and establish its potential as a transmission medium.
summary: This paper experimentally proves that Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF) is a superior transmission medium for quantum networks compared to standard Single-Mode Fiber (SMF). By demonstrating that HCF suppresses nonlinear crosstalk noise by two orders of magnitude, it allows for the reliable co-propagation of high-fidelity quantum entanglement alongside high-capacity classical DWDM signals.
main_problem: The primary challenge is enabling the coexistence of quantum entanglement signals and high-power classical data signals in optical fibers without suffering from nonlinear crosstalk.
main_result: The study experimentally demonstrates that Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF) significantly suppresses background nonlinear noise compared to standard Single-Mode Fiber (SMF), thereby preserving high-fidelity entanglement distribution even when co-propagating with dense Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (DWDM) classical signals.
method: The authors performed direct experimental comparisons between HCF and SMF using polarization-entangled photons alongside high-power DWDM classical signals, measuring entanglement fidelity and background noise.
model_or_system: The experiment compares two physical platforms: standard Single-Mode Fiber (SMF) and Photonic-Bandgap-based Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF). The system involves transmitting polarization-entangled states ($\Psi^+$) alongside classical signals across multiple DWDM channels.
key_observables: Entanglement Fidelity ($F$), background noise count rates, and the degree of nonlinear crosstalk.
important_parameters: Total classical launch power of 11.2 dBm; the noise suppression factor (approximately two orders of magnitude improvement in HCF over SMF).
main_assumptions: The advantage of HCF is attributed to its intrinsically low optical nonlinearity, which is confirmed even after correcting for simple transmission loss differences.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup showing co-propagation, the optical spectrum confirming nonlinear processes (FWM, Raman scattering), and a direct comparison of background noise count rates between HCF and SMF as a function of classical power.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for coexisting quantum/classical light, presents the experimental setup comparing HCF and SMF, measures noise and fidelity under high classical power, and concludes that HCF is superior for maintaining quantum signal integrity.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering bottleneck in quantum networking—the interaction between high-power classical infrastructure and fragile quantum signals—providing crucial empirical data for the deployment of quantum repeaters and quantum internet links.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Schematic of the whole setup. The transmission fiber channel (both HCF and SMF) is deployed underground in the Shin-Kawasaki campus of Keio University, and the fiber length is about 500 m. EDFA: erbium-doped fiber amplifier, BPF: bandpass filter, SMF: single-mode fiber, HCF: hollow-core fiber, DM: dichroic mirror, PBS: polarizing beam splitter, HWP: half-wave plate, QWP: quarter-wave plate, SPDC: spontaneous parametric down-conversion, SSPD: superconducting single-photon detector.
Fig. 2. Outputs of the optical spectrum analyzer and the transmission characteristic of our DWDM filter.

Fig. 3. Measured background noise for SMF (top) and HCF (bottom). The left panels show the SSPD count rates measured using the quantum-signal detection setup. The right panels show measurements obtained by replacing the DWDM filter with a wavelength-tunable filter.

Fig. 4. Reconstructed density matrices of the polarization-entangled state (a) before transmission and after transmission together with classical communication signals through (b) HCF and (c) SMF. The real and imaginary parts are shown in the left and right columns, respectively. Fidelities to the target Bell state are calculated as F = ⟨Ψ+|𝜌|Ψ+⟩, where 𝜌is the reconstructed density matrix.
